item.title: The Uncanny Happiness of Common Unhappiness
item.description:
Happiness

The Uncanny Happiness of Common Unhappiness

What the psychotherapy patient can and cannot realistically expect from therapy.

Posted July 15, 2026

Key points
  • Happiness is a subjective, elusive, and ephemeral state of mind.
  • What makes one person happy may make someone else miserable.
  • Happiness is not the absence of suffering so much as the presence of satisfaction and contentment.
Source: ID 6112869 on Rawpixels

Part 1 of a Series

"Even a happy life cannot be without a measure of darkness, and the word happy would lose its meaning if it were not balanced by sadness."—C.G. Jung

"Much has been gained if we succeed in turning . . . [neurotic] misery into common unhappiness."—Sigmund Freud

"Happiness" can be an ambiguous, amorphous, enigmatic, ephemeral, and elusive concept, construct, and phenomenon. Yet, like the Holy Grail, it is something humans seem to possess an archetypal desire to pursue, discover, and experience. Indeed, when initially asked about their reason for seeking psychotherapy, patients will often respond: "I just want to be happy." Indeed, most if not all psychotherapy is, at some level, about the conscious or unconscious quest for happiness or, at least, less unhappiness. If we are willing to be honest with ourselves, happiness, or at least our own version of it, is what we all want and persistently strive for.

Unhappy people have been seeking the assistance of psychotherapy for more than a century. First, it was Freud's psychoanalysis, where sufferers from sundry symptoms would lie prone on a comfy couch and "free associate," saying aloud whatever entered awareness without judging, editing, or censoring themselves, unburdening their misery, sadness, painful memories, and current concerns and symptoms; and the analyst, unseen and sitting behind them, out of sight, intently and empathically listened, mostly in silence, for months, years, or, in some cases, decades. Eventually, many started to feel better, more content, less symptomatic, and perhaps even a bit happier. Why?

For one thing, there was, and still is, the confessional quality of the process, not unlike that of the Catholic Church, in which the person shares their darkest fantasies, desires, sins, misdemeanors, and even evil deeds in confidence with another human without fearing condemnation, excommunication, or rejection. Something is healing and liberating in receiving such unconditional acceptance, as psychologist Carl Rogers later demonstrated, and it can serve to help a person learn to be more accepting and loving toward oneself and others.

Confronting the Dark Side

Patients in psychoanalysis and modern depth psychology are encouraged to consciously acknowledge and accept their most primitive, primal, and destructive impulses rather than rejecting, censoring, and repressing these powerful, all-too-human instincts such as sexuality and aggression. Moreover, Freud recognized that unhappy, miserable, or neurotic individuals "suffer from reminiscences"—that they tend to constantly carry the traumatic past around with them consciously and unconsciously, dragging them down and keeping them from living freely and fully in the present and future. Thus, one secret to happiness, suggests depth psychology, is that the more we can learn to face and accept our "dark side," what Freud referred to as the "id" (or originally, "it") and Jung poetically spoke of as the "shadow" and to let go of the past, the happier, or at least less unhappy, we can become. Freud, ever the realist (some say pessimist), succinctly described the goal of psychoanalysis as being to transform neurotic "misery into common unhappiness."

article continues after advertisement

For Freud, happiness is a very relative and elusive state given the often tragic nature of the human condition; it is correlated closely with liberation from neurotic guilt, repression, self-condemnation, and others. And, on the plus side, the freedom to work, create, and to give and receive love. In this sense, the less dissatisfaction, frustration, discontent, and neurotic suffering we feel, the happier we become. Happiness, then, could be defined as the relative absence of things about which we are unhappy in life, though there will always be something. Decreasing our unhappiness enhances our happiness. How can this be accomplished? Clearly, this approach requires cultivating a more accepting attitude toward life as it truly is, not how we want it to be, and letting go of grievances and dissatisfaction with the world, others, and ourselves.

Social Interest and Courage as Keys to Happiness

One of Freud's Viennese colleagues and contemporaries, Alfred Adler, who created what he called Individual Psychology, placed a strong emphasis on the concept of "social interest" as key to human happiness. Adler felt that happiness depended in large part on our social interactions, sense of belonging, constructive engagement and participation in society, and genuine concern and care for others and the human community. Central to Adler's approach was the concept of courage: Having the necessary courage to take risks, face daunting challenges, create intimate relationships, pursue one's dreams, and be oneself authentically. For Adler, our happiness hinges significantly on how we relate to society and our fellow human beings, and how much courage we have to creatively carve out a fulfilling and satisfying place for ourselves in the collective culture.

For Otto Rank, another of Freud's close colleagues, creativity is a core ingredient for happiness. This includes not only the artist's creativity but also every person's responsibility to create him or herself and the world through "acts of will," which, when frustrated, blocked, or resisted, result in the dysphoria (unhappiness) and symptomatic suffering of neurosis. In this regard, courageously expressing oneself and one's will in the world creatively--in whatever way one can, be it artistically, in one's work or career, by creating a family, supportive network of friends, intimate relationships, etc.--is essential to human happiness.

These basic concepts of Adler and Rank—the necessity of living courageously and creatively, of being fully engaged in life and in our inextricable social context—can also be found in the contemporary practice of existential therapy, accompanied by a major focus on the importance of meaning and purpose in life. Existential therapy, like the European existential philosophy that informs it, is often mistakenly associated solely with doom, gloom, nihilism, and despair—the opposite of happiness. It too contributes to the cultivation of happiness by encouraging acceptance of certain existential facts of life—anxiety, aloneness, loss, suffering, guilt, finitude, responsibility, meaninglessness, and mortality. Paradoxically, it is when we deny and try to escape from these non-negotiable facts of life that we suffer from symptoms such as neurotic anxiety and depression that tend to degrade and diminish our happiness. However, when we are willing to courageously confront these existential givens, accepting and coming to terms with rather than suppressing or running from them, we become more receptive and open to "savor and be fully present to life's sublime pleasures, beauties, and wonders" (Diamond, 2015, p. 346). But how does this subtle, gradual, sometimes imperceptible transformation toward happiness actually happen in therapy? (See Part 2.)

item.title: Do You Say to Yourself “They Hurt Me?” Read This First
item.description:
Forgiveness

Do You Say to Yourself “They Hurt Me?” Read This First

You forgive people for “wronging” you, yet they are often “righting” you.

Posted July 15, 2026

Key points
  • You forgive people for “wronging” you when, in the long term, they are often “righting” you.
  • “Things happen. You can’t change that. It is up to you to see if you can find a reason.
  • Being grateful, doesn’t mean things happen for a reason. It means things happen. Whether we like it or not.
  • Some of the people you perceive to have hurt you may actually be playing an unexpected role in your growth.

Whether it’s political divisions, the threat of AI to future jobs, economic inequality, or even World Cup referee calls, our culture encourages us to make constant decisions around who was right, who was wrong, and whom we should blame. Has judgment-laden cancel culture fomented an instinct within us that has gradually constructed the walls of the invisible prison cells in which so many of us live?

I will now offer a different possibility: Some of the people and changing conditions you may perceive as hurting you may actually be playing an unexpected role in your growth and, further, that forgiveness is not about rewriting what has happened to you, but about reconsidering and infusing it with new meaning.

Perhaps You Haven’t Been Wronged After All

The approaches to forgiveness that imbue our culture focus on how the other person has “wronged,” “harmed,” or “hurt” us. In her book The Sweet Spot, for example, Berkeley sociologist Christine Carter suggests that the reader write a letter of forgiveness. She gives the example of such a letter culminating with “I forgive you for hurting me in the way that you did.”

While Carter’s book offers otherwise helpful advice on living a meaningful life, ask yourself if you would welcome receiving such a letter. If you bristle at the idea, it is because it is filled with judgment.

Why? “You hurt me” is the forgiver's message. “I am the unequivocal authority on right and wrong and have determined that what occurred between us is your fault. I now forgive you.”

Moments of reflection can transform painful experiences into opportunities for growth.
Source: Unsplash / Keenan Constance

Could You Have Been “Righted?”

You forgive people for “wronging” you when, in the long term, they are often “righting” you. You forgive someone for showing up and being the interaction partner you needed at the time, so you could learn and grow and clarify what you value.

While going through the suffering wrought by this form of learning is no walk in the park, neither is the alternative—staying at home and forgoing learning and growth—such an attractive option.

As I write in my book Love and Suffering: Break the Emotional Chains that Prevent You from Experiencing Love, when you feel you have been “wronged,” further introspection over time may reveal that you have actually been “righted.”

You don’t forgive another person for “wronging” you; you also thank them for enabling you to learn and grow. “The only real meaning of forgiveness,” the author John Demartini writes, “is thank you for giving me this experience.”

article continues after advertisement

Things Happen

I must add a caveat that some horrific events cannot be reappraised in this way. No person, for example, will ever tell you they were “righted” by a loved one being harmed by another person or succumbing to a painful, intractable illness. If you tell someone in such a situation, “Things happen for a reason,” you may lose a friend and will certainly lose your influence.

The wiser counsel in such extremely tragic circumstances: “Things happen. You can’t change that. It is up to you to see if you can find a reason amid such trauma that enables you to continue living and, possibly, if you are very fortunate, to grow.”

According to the Sufis, if you are walking in a garden and step on a thorn, you must remember to say thank you. Yet while you are likely not grateful for everything, shares David Steindl-Rast, who has been a Benedictine monk for the past 70 years, you can be grateful in every moment.

You are not grateful for every event (losing someone), but you can be grateful for being alive and having the capability to learn from every event in your life. The truth is that these two are interrelated: it is your capacity to learn and find meaning in your tragedies that enables you to feel alive.

Being grateful, then, doesn’t mean things happen for a reason. It means things happen. Whether we like it or not. Once they happen, it is up to you to determine what you can learn from them—how you can move forward in your life wiser, stronger, more resolute—with the benefit of the lessons these events have shown up in your life to teach you.

Resilience emerges when individuals choose to find meaning and wisdom in adversity, allowing difficult experiences to become catalysts for strength and personal transformation.
Source: Vladislav Babienko / Unsplash

item.title: Wordplay Is Play but Mistakes Can Be Symptoms
item.description:
Aphasia

Wordplay Is Play but Mistakes Can Be Symptoms

Humorous slips of the tongue are separate from symptomatic speech errors.

Posted July 15, 2026

Key points
  • Spoonerisms, swapping letters and syllables, are often funny, fun, and harmless.
  • Other speech errors may indicate serious neurological issues.

When the Reverend William Archibald Spooner, the kindly Oxford-educated scholar and priest, called for his congregation to sing the venerable 19th-century Church of England hymn “Conquering Kings Their Titles Take,” it came out “Kinkering Congs.”

He may be unfairly remembered for slips of the tongue like this because he might not even have made this mistake. Or he might have misspoken this way only once. Or, not quite the dithering ancient scholar he portrayed, he may have played along, inventing new, playful “Spoonerisms.” Whatever the case, the mistake became a namesake.

The notorious word-mangler, William Archibald Spooner, caricatured.
Source: A Leslie Ward cartoon via Wikipedia from Vanity Fair (April, 1898)

Mistake Becomes Namesake

Spooner’s students (as gifted, mischievous students will) delighted in manufacturing mistakes like his, piling on, contributing to the legend. The students’ inventions, though, are often funnier than the original.

In one sermon, Spooner is alleged to have tried to say, “Our Lord is a Loving Shepherd.” It didn’t take much switching around to make him say, “Our Lord is a Shoving Leopard.” Or when reproving a student for lax attendance and attempting to say, “You have missed all of my history lectures” instead he came out with “You have hissed all of my mystery lectures!”

Here are a couple that I like even more. Allegedly, when performing a wedding ceremony and attempting to intone the traditional “it is customary to kiss the bride,” he inadvertently said, “it is kisstomary to cuss the bride.” And then the one everybody likes best: meaning to refer to “our dear old Queen,” to the assembled congregants, he bumbled on to “our queer old Dean.”

Humorists who swap syllables for a laugh will still be said to commit a “Spoonerism,” wordplay of a specific kind where consonants or vowels or syllables are switched or added. A stale sandwich at a diner? Try “chilled grease” for grilled cheese.

A Night at the Opera

Or the scene in the Marx Brothers film A Night at the Opera that turns on a pun and a near spoonerism. Groucho, as the slippery character Otis B. Driftwood, parses the legalese in a bogus document he wants Chico to sign.

article continues after advertisement

Groucho begins reading the fine print. “It says…” he squints, “if any of the parties participating in this contract is shown not to be in their right mind, the entire agreement is automatically nullified.”

Chico is skeptical. Groucho, weaseling to reassure him, explains “that’s what they call a sanity clause.”

“You can’t fool me,” Chico snickers, “there ain’t no Sanity Klause!”

Your Spoonerism Generator

Spoonerisms circulate as puns, switching initial letters or pairs of consonants. “Runny babbit” for bunny rabbit, for instance, or “bunny phone” for “funny bone.”

Therapists can try their tongues on Spoonerisms. A patient might need to fight the blues. Feed it through a do-it-yourself Spoonerism generator, and it delivers “bite the flues.” Or similarly, a half-formed wish becomes “a half-warmed fish.” Go ahead and try it. Run through the alphabet with paired words. A “smart feller” becomes a…

Spoonerisms shouldn’t be confused with mistakes that arise from a failure of preparation or an underdeveloped vocabulary. Extemporaneous speakers often try and miss catching words that lie just out of reach. These deserve our sympathy. (Would you want your offhand remarks transcribed and scrutinized?)

But public mistakes from professional talkers are not soon forgotten. When introducing Hubert Horatio Humphrey, the former Vice President, at the Democratic National Convention, President Jimmy Carter called him “Hubert Horatio Hornblower,” recalling a character in a naval adventure novel. (And to call a cheery, talkative politico hornblower, well….) The 43rd president, George W. Bush, so dependably blundered into the mangled or invented word that wits collected a stack of “Bushisms.” He complained about being “misunderestimated,” for example.

article continues after advertisement

Word Substitution as Symptom

The rest of us, especially as we move along, will be prone to inadvertence, minor forgetfulness, more trouble multitasking, and slower recall.

Where did I put my glasses? How did she beat me to that Jeopardy answer? So much is ordinary. An older writer may strain for le mot juste. What’s a synonym for nonplussed? Unbothered? No. Umm. How about bewildered…? Maybe settle for “stumped.” OK. Let’s go with stumped…

But if one routinely leaves the car keys in the refrigerator rather than the jacket pocket, or if one has trouble finding the way back from the grocery store, something more serious than slow recall may be afoot.

Prominent people who have suffered brain injuries more often publicly struggle with language difficulties. Their stories range from heartbreak to resilience.

After the action film star Bruce Willis began to forget his lines on set, neurologists diagnosed incipient frontotemporal dementia. Sharon Stone, who famously played the lead in the thriller Basic Instinct, experienced a serious brain bleed that required years of therapy to recover fluent speech. After filming the first season of Game of Thrones, Emilia Clarke experienced two brain hemorrhages; her foundation SameYou helps fellow patients with long-term recovery.

An estimated two million Americans recovering from brain injury suffer degrees of aphasia, a speech disorder. High-profile public figures who have experienced insults to the brain that left their speech impaired include former congresswoman Gabby Giffords, the victim of an attempted assassination. Pennsylvania Senator John Fetterman needed the assistance of real-time closed captioning after a stroke left him with language-processing difficulties.

While in office, Woodrow Wilson suffered a stroke that garbled his speech and impaired his thinking for the remaining 17 months of his presidency. During this interval, aides were partly successful in covering up his disability. His wife Edith controlled the flow of information to Wilson, serving as his “steward,” she said. Her role became so crucial to the affairs of state that some historians regard her as the first female President.

Evidence From Speech Patterns

Speech-language pathologists and neuropsychologists do not need brain imagery or a battery of clinical tests to begin to raise concern about a patient’s cognitive decline. Specific patterns of expression are sufficient indicators.

Garrulous individuals who are recurrently in the public eye (public ear?) and who are easily observed and heard may catch the attention of experts in mental decline.

article continues after advertisement

Substituting similar-sounding words or non-words for intended words, a form of disturbance called phonemic paraphasia, will go unnoticed or unregarded in most people most of the time. Sometimes these appear unintentionally but humorously. For example, meaning to say “dishwasher” and saying “wishdasher” instead.

Were this mistake a symptom of underlying disease, however, it would be called an example of phonemic paraphasia—one of several related word-retrieval symptoms.

Public mistakes before audiences are easily observed and, again, not soon forgotten. Codes of best practice, however, strongly caution psychiatrists who are tempted to diagnose pathology from afar and without the benefit of testing.

But if a public figure under routine scrutiny is heard speaking literal gibberish at a press conference, or uses non-words at a rally or a debate, experts from another field—speech-language pathology—have their ears tuned. They may detect evidence of “phonemic paraphasia” and may sound an early warning of stroke that has damaged the language centers of the brain, or they may suspect incipient Alzheimer’s disease or progressing frontotemporal dementia.

Here are some familiar examples from the current president, now in his 81st year.

Substituting a real but incorrect word for an intended, similar-sounding word, President Donald Trump referred to the “Islamic Republic of Japan.” Similarly, he noted that by working two or three jobs every day, parents may “sacrifice the furniture of their children.” Saying Leon instead of “Elon,” “oranges” instead of “origins,” and slurring “bigly” for “big league” are more errors of this kind. Speech language pathologists hear in these mistakes in sounds instances of phonemic paraphasia.

article continues after advertisement

Phonemic paraphasia is not wordplay.

The Behavioral Variant

The trouble with prefrontal brain damage, alas, is not only linguistic. More alarmingly, age-related mental decline can also vary and manifest in observable, troubling behavior.

Typically, as the neural connections in the front of the brain begin to deteriorate, affected individuals will also become more impulsive, more “disinhibited,” and more prone to inappropriate social conduct. Judgment suffers. Sufferers may confabulate and lie. They will ramble. They fixate. They taunt. As empathy wanes and hostility replaces nuance, they also often swear more frequently.

When the language networks located on both sides of the front of the brain begin to fail, and as executive functions begin to weaken, such sufferers speak (and thus think) more starkly and simplistically.

Spoonerisms will tickle our bunny phones, but the prospect of prefrontal dementia is not at all funny.

item.title: Don't Rush Into Couples Therapy
item.description:
Therapy

Don't Rush Into Couples Therapy

Here's how to tell if you would be better served by individual work.

Posted July 15, 2026

Key points
  • Couple's therapy can be useful if properly screened.
  • Many issues presenting in couple's therapy are better addressed individually.
  • Emotional, values, and attachment styles are frequently handled more effectively in individual therapy.

In couples’ therapy, we tend to see people arriving in a crisis or emergency situation in need of a referee or mediator. Sometimes, couples come to therapy 5 or 10 years too late. When resentment has grown into contempt, there is little a therapist can do.

In many cases, however, the challenges people come to couples therapy with are better served through individual work, which can often be screened in an intake.

Below are four signs that you may be better served by individual therapy to manage and repair issues in your relationship.

1. You have difficulty being alone without your partner

We might begin some relationships as a response or reflex away from an insecure or uncomfortable feeling within. We feel restless or unhappy when we are alone, and being near a partner and having them with us can feel like a satisfying end to this loneliness.

Over time, this can lead to enmeshment or what used to be called co-dependence: an inability to properly separate or differentiate yourself from your partner.

This can manifest as anxiety, restlessness, irritability, or an inability to pull away, take a timeout, or let things “ferment” on their own. While many believe the myth of “not going to bed angry,” the reality is that some issues are not resolvable in an evening, and more communication and more attention can do damage to your fragile bond.

Having a moratorium on contentious issues, with a promise to revisit them, can be a helpful strategy. However, if this experience of separation causes severe pain for an individual, they may need to process and explore that first with a separate party rather than their partner.

2. You have difficulty identifying and naming your emotions

Many people struggle to name the affects they are feeling at a given moment. They know that something feels bad or “off” but cannot isolate it concretely as “rejection,” “suspicion,” or “rage.”

This lack of specificity and differentiation often bleeds over into their partner, whom they assume must be responsible for how they are feeling. Their partner may be the nearest person and thus the most obvious culprit.

This can also lead to an error of attribution, confusing the person for a behavior—“you are cruel and aggressive” rather than “that behavior felt cruel and aggressive.” This is hard to sort out when in the throes of conflict, since our brains often regress to fight-or-flight very easily and thus cannot perform the careful cognitive differentiation required for this action. An individual therapist provides a safer environment to sort out this difference.

article continues after advertisement

3. You do not have a strong sense of your own values

When we enter relationships, we often subconsciously enter into shared value systems or unstated agreements. We may defer to our partner’s values out of a sense of attachment desire—to make them happy or to ensure relational continuity.

Over time, partners who have not explicitly revised their goals and values as a couple can build resentment and values confusion. Am I living the life that I need and want? Have I compromised too much?

Sorting out one’s authentic, individual values and debating and discussing them with one’s partner are keys to long-term monogamous stability and health. This can be achieved as a couple, though sometimes there is fear of disappointing the other with renewed or revised life goals. Here again, individual therapy may be preferable to a couples approach.

4. You isolate and shut down easily

Finally, if you or your partner repeatedly and consistently shuts down or withdraws when there is conflict, this may prove an obstacle to couple work. Resentments may be too entrenched or habits too well formed. Moreover, if our partner points this out, it can often lead to further regression and stonewalling, as it can feel like another attack or criticism.

A third party can often identify the patterns and their origins in family relationships. Most often, patterns like this are rooted deep in family of origin issues—you may have shut down to prevent dad from raging. Or you may have observed this pattern in dad himself, as he withdrew from mother’s criticism rather than debate her directly.

When a therapist identifies these patterns, the client may feel less threatened and may be able to try out strategies and review them in the safety pod of therapy.

In all cases, it is important to remember that couples therapy is not advised for every couple. In many cases, highly conflictual or avoidant couples may, in fact, do more damage to themselves and their relationship in the process of therapy.

item.title: After the Blast, a Soldier Learns to Sleep Again
item.description:
Complex PTSD

After the Blast, a Soldier Learns to Sleep Again

Ukraine's Vsesylni clinic treats the brain, body, and wounds no one can see.

Posted July 15, 2026

Key points
  • Art therapy can open doors that words cannot.
  • Blast injuries need teams, not single specialists.
  • For a traumatized brain, sleep is a major victory.

The Man Everyone Thought Was Dead

For three days after a landmine blast near Bakhmut, Sasha lay unconscious. He had been so gravely wounded that he was thought dead. He regained consciousness inside a black body bag in a morgue. Sasha — not his real name — was injured in May 2023. The explosion caused severe facial injuries and traumatic brain injury. By the time he arrived at Vsesylni, a rehabilitation clinic in Odesa, he had endured six operations. One side of his face was partly paralyzed, and he was so self-conscious about his appearance that he was on his way to becoming a recluse.

The damage that could not be seen was equally disabling. He had headaches, tinnitus, insomnia, depression, and an intense sensitivity to light, all common after traumatic brain injury. "He is a very strong man," said Olga Peskova, founder of Vsesylni. But strength had not taught his injured brain how to become quiet.

A Key to Accepting Mental Health Support

Like many Ukrainian servicemen, Sasha was not eager to accept psychotherapy. Because of the abuse of psychiatry under the Soviets, who used psychiatry as a tool of political repression and confined dissidents in hospitals, psychotherapy in Ukraine carries a lingering reputation as an instrument of control rather than care.

Peskova has found, however, that some soldiers who are reluctant to get mental health support will accept physical rehabilitation, massage, or treatment for scars — and once they feel safe, this opens the door to mental health care. For Sasha, that door opened during an art therapy session led by Rosie Cecil, Vsesylni's head of international partnerships. The soldiers had been asked to create mandalas — circular, often colorful designs that can provide a calming focus for reflection.

Mandala created by a patient at Vsesylni
Source: Olga Peskova, used with permission

In both Peskova's and Cecil's experience, art can be especially useful when people aren't yet able to put into words what they are going through. A person who cannot yet talk about an unbearable memory may be able to express it indirectly through color, shape, and symbol.

The colors of Sasha's mandala were red and black. Peskova, watching him work, understood what those colors meant to him: red for blood, black for death. What he could not yet say aloud, his hands had said for him. It was also clear to her that he would need psychotherapy — and, crucially, that enough trust had now been established that he would be willing to accept it.

article continues after advertisement

Treating the Whole Injury

Patients at the clinic can stay for 14 days. During that time, Sasha saw psychotherapists, a neurologist, and physiotherapists, and took part in group therapy. He also received transcranial magnetic stimulation and EEG neurofeedback—what Peskova calls "gymnastics for the brain and nervous system," a description that turns out to be more literal than it sounds.

In a neurofeedback session, specialists placed small sensors on Sasha's scalp to pick up his brain's electrical activity, or brainwaves. The sensors pick up important clues. A traumatic brain injury can throw the brain's rhythms out of balance, trapping the brain in states of hyperarousal, with too many fast, agitated waves driving anxiety and sleeplessness, or in the slow, foggy patterns associated with depression.

During the neurofeedback sessions, a computer translated whatever his brain was doing into something he could see on a screen and hear in real time: a video that brightens or dims, a tone that rises or falls. Ideally, over repeated sessions, the brain can notice the connection between its own activity and the feedback it receives and begin to adjust. The underlying principle is neuroplasticity, the brain's capacity to rewire itself. Sasha’s neurofeedback sessions were designed to help with the rewiring.

Peskova feels that the evidence for neurofeedback and repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation after traumatic brain injury has not yet been declared proven. Still, in her experience, it’s promising enough to use, and in many cases like Sasha’s, she’s seen the benefits.

Some of what Vsesylni does may not yet be proven; however, the overall principle behind everything the clinic does is well-established: a brain injury that touches sleep, mood, cognition, and the body all at once cannot be handed off to a single specialist and called treated. U.S. military and veterans' guidelines have reached the same conclusion: Soldiers with chronic, overlapping symptoms tend to fare better under a coordinated, team-based plan.

The reasoning for this approach is clear. Pain disrupts sleep. Lost sleep undermines mood and the ability to think. A disfigured face drives a man indoors, away from the human contact that might otherwise help him heal. And psychological trauma can make physical pain feel worse than it is. The multi-therapy approach worked for Sasha.

article continues after advertisement

"I'm Sleeping Now"

At the end of the program, Sasha gave Peskova an encouraging report: "I'm sleeping now." He also said his headaches had stopped and the noise in his injured ear had subsided. The man who once awakened among the dead is not finished healing. However, both Peskova and Cecil have seen that Sasha has begun to believe again that living is worth it.

item.title: Was It Really Love?
item.description:
Relationships

Was It Really Love?

Personal Perspective: A perfectionist's misunderstanding of what true love is.

Posted July 15, 2026

Key points
  • To feel loved, perfectionists tend to have extreme standards for others.
  • They struggle with heartbreak because it causes them to doubt whether they were ever loved to begin with.
  • Addressing the confusion at a relationship's end can help you make sense of its meaning.

Two years ago, I dated someone I really connected with. We had great banter, I found her extremely attractive, and I thought about her all the time. I was under the impression that we shared similar feelings for each other, especially considering her compliments to me. One day, however, she broke it off, telling me she was hoping for a stronger connection. Automatically, I panicked. I thought, “I was wrong about everything. I completely misread her.” Months after the relationship’s end, I continued to struggle with the thought: “Did she really like me?” The relationship’s end wiped out every positive thought I had about it and myself. I couldn’t believe how wrong I was about its direction. I was wrong that it was going well.

While my heartbreak is obviously common, my inability to emotionally process it wasn’t. And while I blamed my former partner for making me dislike myself, I meaningfully contributed to my self-concept. To have believed her compliments, I needed perfection. After breakups, patients frequently ask others, especially their therapists, “Were we even really in love?” The answer might be an obvious “yes” to others, but the devastated individual struggles with understanding how love can both be genuine and temporary. It’s easier to assume you’ve just been duped or, in the worst-case scenario, unlovable. Seldom questioned is your standard of “true love.”

When I say I needed perfection in my experience, I mean I needed everything to line up: My partner’s words, deeds, and thoughts had to be consistent, always. Otherwise, I had extreme doubt about the relationship. When she told me she hoped for a stronger connection, I was certain she never felt anything for me. And I didn’t know whether to blame her for misleading me or myself for misunderstanding her. Confusion is perfectionism’s core emotion because, again, everything is supposed to line up to make sense.

What are you supposed to do when it doesn’t? Me? I run. Whether my partner did or didn’t like me wasn’t as important as my tendency to avoid complex, emotional problems. I assumed the relationship was founded on a false perception of it because doing so afforded me three gifts:

  1. I now believed I had a clear understanding of our relationship.
  2. I didn’t have to continue making sense of what went wrong, including my contributions, and further try to tolerate the feeling of confusion (I could tell myself that she just never liked me from the start and begin trying to move on).
  3. I allowed myself to avoid future heartbreak and further confirmation (or worse, indisputable proof) of being unlovable by telling myself, “It just doesn’t work for me.”

But that wasn’t true; that relationship wasn’t based on a false belief about it. It was true, however, that I wanted clarity more than anything else while in it. I wanted her affection to never waver. I wanted to know that she thought and felt only good thoughts and feelings about me, always. For the perfectionist, perfection is just as often demanded from one’s circumstances as it is from oneself. It’s one thing to expect consistency from a partner, meaning that another’s thoughts and actions line up for the most part, but I didn’t just want her to like me with the occasional interpersonal rupture; I wanted her to worship me, almost. And to overlook anything that would’ve likely irritated anyone else. To feel emotionally secure, I needed her to happily tolerate every annoying and even hurtful thing I said and did or, even better, somehow appreciate it.

article continues after advertisement

While there’s some validity to my needs, again, they were exorbitant. I can expect someone to stay to work out our conflicts; I can’t expect them to accept everything I choose to do—passively. Looking back, I realize she legitimately felt some degree of affection for me, but she was a perfectionist, too. Her not feeling a strong connection was about her—as much as it was about me. With respect to my own perfectionism, my problem was in defining love nonsensically. And I used that notion of true love as a standard to prove whether or not I was lovable. In doing that, I lost the possibility of deeply knowing her, her needs, and even internal barriers to intimacy. Fixated on my pain, I was unable to find a way to navigate the rupture between us; I walked away without trying because it was easy.

I walked away feeling unlovable but self-righteous. I hated her for breaking me, and I somehow simultaneously believed I could and couldn’t do better than her—I knew (ideally) I deserved better treatment but remained skeptical about finding it (realistically). As I remained locked in my mind, in my very rigid perspectives, I missed what I was incapable of providing her, at least then. She needed empathy and my willingness to see past my own hurt (at least temporarily) to help her with hers, even though, at that point, it likely didn’t mean continuing our relationship. Perfectionism can be thought of as a rigid and excessive attempt to cultivate self-love. But, while you try to create that sort of love in your mind, you inadvertently and carelessly destroy the possibility of real love in the real world. Perfectionism, in whichever form, whether toward yourself or your relationship, can just as easily kill your dreams as it creates them.

Was our affection for one another real? I’d say yes. Our inability to work out our problems and understand each other ultimately ended our union. And if you try to believe that a former love of yours was real, too, maybe you can perceive its end in less personal terms. Maybe love sometimes fades, and your confusion isn’t some insurmountable problem. Maybe your anxiety about loving isn’t a harbinger of certainty that you’re forever tainted. Maybe you can start again.

item.title: The Challenges and Opportunities of Divorce
item.description:
Divorce

The Challenges and Opportunities of Divorce

Divorce is about stepping into a new chapter of your life, one you can create.

Posted July 15, 2026

Key points
  • Divorce is a major life event that brings not only transitions and grief but its own challenges.
  • There may be changes in your lifestyle, your relationship with your children, a loss of friends, and anxiety.
  • But with this transition is also an opportunity to set your own goals; create the new chapter that you desire.
Source: Tumisu / Pixabay

Psychologically, divorce is the closing of one chapter of your life and the beginning of a new one. But the shift is never smooth. No matter the circumstances and reasons for the divorce, there is always an undertone of grief and loss, simply because your attachment to someone, whether it be good or bad, healthy or unhealthy, was still a psychological attachment. And when it is severed, grief is a psychological byproduct.

But this transition to a new chapter brings even more challenges. Knowing what to expect reduces anxiety and worry about what’s next. Here are some of the most common and normal consequences of divorce:

You feel miserable; you also feel relieved

For at least several weeks, your moods may go up and down. On a good day, you feel relieved to be away from all those stressors and problems. On a bad day, especially when grief rears up, you question whether you did the right thing.

Your lifestyle has changed

The rented apartment, the tight budget. No more fancy dinners or vacations in the near future. On a bad day, it all fuels self-doubt and questions whether you made the right decision.

Children are struggling

Hopefully not, but children are marching through the same life chapter change with less control. Here, children may get depressed or act out. Or your relationship with them changes in a major way: they may blame you for the divorce, or, more commonly, one child is supportive while the other is hateful. Either way, you have a challenge on your hands to help your children move forward, get over this big hiccup in their lives, and avoid lasting damage.

You lose friends

The quandary for friends of couples is that they struggle as well. Those who are lifelong friends of yours stay friends. Those who were tied to your ex drop out or keep minimal contact. Those in the middle may stay there as long as they can, but it doesn’t erase the awkwardness on both sides—another challenge to move through.

You look at your past through a new lens

You can’t be divorced and simultaneously look back and think your relationship was wonderful. The past and present need to match. So now, when you wake up at 3 a.m., you think about all those red flags you swept under the rug before—the argument on the third date; Christmas 2016 and how they treated your mother.

article continues after advertisement

Real facts that didn’t seem important before now stand out in bold relief. Again, it makes sense. Your brain doesn’t like cognitive dissonance.

Old losses rear up

You find yourself drifting back to your big breakup in high school or college, the death of your parent, your regrets about not speaking up in your first marriage, or that you did speak up at a cost. Like knots on a rope, all losses are connected; one triggers the others.

You feel like a 16-year-old

If you’re beginning to date, even though you know intellectually that you’ve grown and are a wiser and more competent adult, those initial steps can feel like being back in high school, with all its awkwardness and worry about making the right impression. You feel like a teen because, emotionally, in some ways, you are.

How to move forward

So, how do you combat these challenges? Here are some suggestions:

  • Be generous with yourself. Give yourself some grace. Accept that you’re going through a major life event. Be kind to yourself; realize that your emotions will be unsettled for a few months.
  • Know that children are resilient. Most children are more flexible than you think, and in today’s world, perhaps unfortunately, they know they are not alone: they have classmates going through the same thing, and teachers understand that they need some TLC and can empathize and provide support. What they need from you is some sense of regularity, safety, and ongoing support.
  • Control your anxiety. It’s easy to feel overwhelmed, as if everything is important. This is your anxiety talking. The antidote is to step back, engage your rational brain, and set priorities. It’s time to get support from friends, a therapist, a minister, or a doctor. Someone who can understand and keep you moving forward.
  • Change the story. Divorce isn’t about failure but about growth. The box you were in no longer fits. It isn’t about scolding yourself or obsessing over mistakes, but about turning a page in your life. You’re in charge of creating the story; change it, and you can change.
  • Learn the lessons. If you believe your life is working for you, not against you, then believe there’s a moral to the story of your past relationship. This is about you, not the other. It’s not about being a victim but about learning to run your life differently.
article continues after advertisement

An opportunity for change

During times of transition, you can feel most vulnerable, but it’s also a time when your life is most fluid and open to change. This is the time to apply those lessons, step back, and decide how you want to be, what is important, and what you need to create the life you desire.

If you’re simply running away, that old self will follow, and you’ll repeat history. If you’re running toward something new, it can become your guiding light. Use it as a beacon. Grab hold and take advantage of this time.
